channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan's GDP fell at an annualised 0.1% in July–September, the first contraction in four quarters, with private consumption down 0.3%, more than the 0.2% fall expected, preliminary Cabinet Office data show.
item.description:
Japan's gross domestic product fell at an annualised rate of 0.1% in the July–September quarter, according to preliminary Cabinet Office data, The Asahi Shimbun reports. CNA reports that this translated into a quarterly fall of 0.02% and was the first contraction in four quarters, and Beijing Daily that it followed three consecutive quarters of growth. Private consumption, over half of economic output, fell 0.3% against a market estimate of a 0.2% decline, as households tightened their budgets because of higher living costs. The Asahi Shimbun attributes the decline to the increasing cost of oil imports and slowing consumer spending. The rows do not give the contributions of business investment, exports or public spending, or whether the 0.3% consumption figure is quarter on quarter or annualised.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a preliminary estimate of a near-flat quarter. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a small contraction driven by consumption and import costs points to an economy where energy prices are reducing household spending power rather than to a sharp downturn. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japan is a large producer of vehicles, electronics and specialty chemicals, so weak domestic consumption matters mainly for consumer goods and housing, while industrial demand depends more on exports; the rows give no figures on these. Points that may be worth considering include the revised GDP estimate, Japanese industrial output and Bank of Japan statements.

CNA | The Asahi Shimbun | Beijing Daily

item.title: China's industrial output grew 4.8% year on year in October, down from 5.5% in September, and retail sales rose 0.4%, National Bureau of Statistics data show, with industrial robot production up 26%.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that China's National Bureau of Statistics said on 16 November that industrial output grew 4.8% year on year in October, against 5.5% in September, and retail sales rose 0.4% year on year. Services retail sales grew 4.9% in the first ten months, down from 5% in the first three quarters, and the surveyed urban unemployment rate fell to 5.1% from 5.2% in September. A statistics bureau spokesperson said industrial robot production rose 26% year on year in October, while lithium-ion battery production rose 30% and 3D printing equipment production 85.9%, Beijing Daily reports; the row does not state the basis for the last two figures. The rows do not give output by heavy industry, chemicals or construction materials, fixed-asset investment, property data, or market forecasts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report monthly activity data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, slowing industrial growth and near-flat retail sales point to weak domestic demand, while high growth in robots and batteries shows where investment is concentrated. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, China is both a large market and a large producer of raw materials, so weak consumer demand can keep pressure on prices of Chinese intermediates and on export pricing, while electronics, battery and automation production use specialised bonding and potting materials; the rows give no figures for these. Points that may be worth considering include November activity data, fixed-asset investment and Chinese chemical export prices.

MarketScreener | Beijing Daily

item.title: President Trump said on 12 November that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and directed Vice President Vance to focus on domestic politics, The Guardian reports.
item.description:
The Guardian reports that President Trump announced on 12 November that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and directed Vice President Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic politics instead. Middle East Monitor, citing a Washington Post report based on a US official, reports that Trump does not want to resume the war with Iran "for now" while his administration maintains economic and military pressure on Tehran, and that the administration has settled on a middle path of no new war, no talks and no lasting peace. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that Trump publicly reprimanded Vance, who had written on X after election day that the reason for the defeat was the war. The rows do not report an Iranian response, a change in US economic or military pressure on Tehran, or a market reaction to the announcement.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a stated change in US diplomacy, not a change in military operations or trade measures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the end of talks without, for now, a resumption of fighting keeps the current situation in place, including US economic and military pressure on Tehran and the risk to tankers in the region, and reduces the chance of an early settlement. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, energy and petrochemical costs remain exposed to the Gulf, so a longer stalemate keeps a risk premium on oil-derived raw materials and on freight through the region; the rows give no price figures. Points that may be worth considering include the Shenzhen summit agenda, Iranian statements and tanker attack reports.

The Guardian | Middle East Monitor | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: US prices for inputs to new nonresidential construction rose 13.3% in the year to October, with diesel up 115.2%, while overall construction input prices were virtually unchanged from September, contractor associations' analyses show.
item.description:
The Associated General Contractors of America's analysis of producer price data shows the index for inputs to new nonresidential construction rose 13.3% from October 2025 to October 2026, the largest rise in over four years. Diesel fuel more than doubled, up 115.2% over 12 months despite a 4.6% fall from September; liquid asphalt rose 11.5%, truck freight 24.6%, steel mill products 32.9%, copper and brass mill shapes 23.9%, aluminium mill shapes 23.3% and precast concrete products 9.9%. The association notes that metals prices have surged since tariffs of up to 50% were imposed in 2025. The Associated Builders and Contractors' analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price index data shows construction input prices virtually unchanged in October from September, nonresidential input prices up 0.2% on the month, and overall and nonresidential construction materials prices both 11.5% higher than a year earlier; crude petroleum prices fell 10.3% in the month, unprocessed energy materials 7.7%, while natural gas rose 3.7%. The two associations use different series, so their year-on-year figures are not the same measure. The rows give no prices for adhesive technologies or other chemical products.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report input prices, which are a cost measure, not demand. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, flat monthly prices after a year of strong increases suggest that cost pressure on US contractors has stopped rising but stays high, and high input costs can delay or shrink projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction customers facing higher metal, fuel and freight costs may resist price increases on other materials, while the monthly fall in crude petroleum prices is a sign of relief for oil-derived inputs; the rows give no figures for these products. Points that may be worth considering include November producer price data, nonresidential construction spending and freight costs.

Associated General Contractors of America | Associated Builders and Contractors

item.title: Indian domestic passenger vehicle sales rose 12.4% year on year to 519,060 units in October, with two-wheeler sales up 16.1% and three-wheeler sales up 25.7%, SIAM data show, The Economic Times reports.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) recorded a 12.4% year-on-year increase in domestic passenger vehicle sales to 519,060 units in October 2026. Three-wheeler sales rose 25.7% to 103,349 units and two-wheeler sales 16.1% to 2,577,810 units. The row does not give the month-on-month change, the role of the festival season, production or export figures, the split by fuel type, or the year-to-date trend.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports domestic sales by vehicle type for one month. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, one strong month can reflect seasonal buying, so a single figure says less about the trend than several months together. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly uses structural bonding, sealing and coating materials, so rising Indian vehicle sales can support demand from carmakers and their suppliers in India; the row gives no figures on production or materials. Points that may be worth considering include November sales, production data and carmakers' capacity plans in India.

The Economic Times

item.title: The value of Chinese car exports to Germany rose 69% in January–September 2026 against the same period two years earlier, NZZ writes, while Chinese cars' share of new registrations in Germany, France and Switzerland was only 5% to 7%.
item.description:
Neue Zürcher Zeitung writes that the value of Chinese car exports to Germany increased by 69% in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period two years earlier. Over the same timeframe, exports to France doubled and those to Switzerland quadrupled. However, the share of Chinese cars in new registrations in these countries was only 5% to 7%. If Western brands in Chinese hands, such as Polestar and Volvo, are included, the share in Switzerland, where no special tariffs are levied on Chinese cars, rises to around 10%. The row does not give the number of cars, the export values in euros, a separate share for Germany, the share of electric vehicles, or the change against 2025.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row compares export values over two years and gives registration shares; a value is not a volume and a share across three countries is not a German figure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, rising imports at a still low share mean that Chinese brands are gaining ground in Germany without yet changing the market structure, and that competition for German carmakers in their home market is growing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, imported cars are bonded and sealed at plants outside Germany, so a shift of German demand towards imports moves material specification and supply to those plants and their supplier networks; the row gives no figures on this. Points that may be worth considering include KBA registration data by brand origin, EU tariff decisions on Chinese cars and Chinese carmakers' plans for European assembly.

Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: Spain's construction output fell 9.8% year on year in September, the ninth consecutive year-on-year fall, with building construction down 34.7% and civil engineering down 8.6%, National Statistics Institute data show.
item.description:
ABC reports that, according to Spain's National Statistics Institute (INE), the general index of construction production fell 9.8% year on year in September, the same decrease as in August, and construction output has now been down year on year for nine consecutive months. The fall was mainly due to building construction, down 34.7% year on year, while civil engineering fell 8.6% and specialised construction activities 2.7% against September 2025. Adjusted for seasonal and calendar effects, output fell 10.6% year on year, two tenths more than the 10.4% fall in August, and fell 1% from August. The row does not split building into residential and non-residential, give causes, or say how output compares with permits, orders or employment.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a measured output index, not orders or employment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall of more than a third in building output points to lower material use on sites now, and output data can differ from employment figures when work shifts between segments or projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, building construction is a large user of tile adhesives, sealants, flooring adhesives and waterproofing, so a fall concentrated in building rather than civil engineering is more relevant than the headline figure; the row gives no breakdown by building type. Points that may be worth considering include October output, building permits and the split between new build and renovation.

ABC.es

item.title: China's first Double 11 shopping festival under its national standard restricting excessive express packaging is ending, and the standard limits sealing tape width to 45 mm and non-fragile items to two packaging layers.
item.description:
Beijing Daily reports that China's first "Double 11" e-commerce promotion since the national standard "Requirements for Restricting Excessive Express Packaging" took effect is coming to an end. Zhu Lei, a senior engineer at the Beijing Institute of Graphic Communication and director of the State Post Bureau's Green Packaging Technology R&D Center, says the standard restricts excessive packaging and has not lowered the strength requirements for cartons. It sets quantitative requirements in three areas: the suitability of packaging boxes, the number of packaging layers and the amount of sealing tape used, including no more than two layers of packaging for non-fragile and non-breakable items and a tape width of no more than 45 mm. It does not give the date the standard took effect, parcel volumes, the share of shipments that comply, any enforcement or penalties, or measured damage rates.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes a national rule and its quantified limits, not its effect on volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, limits on layers and tape width in China's express parcel market push packers towards fewer materials per shipment, which places more weight on the strength and sealing performance of each box. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, carton sealing tapes, and the adhesives on them, are directly addressed by the tape-width limit, and case and carton closing adhesives can be affected indirectly, so demand can shift towards narrower tapes and closures that hold with less material; the row gives no figures on tape or adhesive use. Points that may be worth considering include parcel damage data after the festival, enforcement practice and similar packaging rules in other markets.

Beijing Daily

item.title: Global oil supply exceeded demand by almost 2 million barrels a day in October, the first time since the Iran war began, and stocks rose 52 million barrels as Gulf exports recovered to 74% of pre-war levels, the IEA says.
item.description:
The International Energy Agency's monthly report, published on 13 November, says global oil supply exceeded demand by almost 2 million barrels a day in October, the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran. Global supply rose 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.36 million, after a 3 million rise in September, driven largely by higher exports from Gulf producers, mainly Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Oil exports from the Gulf states excluding Oman reached 18.4 million barrels a day despite continuing attacks on tankers, 74% of pre-war levels, and global oil stocks rose by 52 million barrels. Dawn reports the IEA expects supply to average 105 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million above its demand forecast. Cinco Días writes that the market is heading for a fourth-quarter surplus of about 2 million barrels a day, against a deficit of a similar amount predicted in last month's report, and that the full year will still end with an average deficit of 685,000 barrels a day, against the 1.7 million the agency calculated a month ago. The IEA forecasts global oil demand to fall 2.7 million barrels a day in 2026, expects demand to rise again from around March 2027, and says petrochemical feedstocks are expected to account for almost 80% of demand growth in 2027. The rows give no price forecast and no figures by product.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report supply, demand, stocks and export volumes, not prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a supply surplus and rising stocks tend to ease crude and refined-product prices, although the attacks on tankers and the 26% gap to pre-war Gulf exports keep the risk of new disruption. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many polymers, resins and solvents are derived from oil and petrochemical feedstocks, so easier oil supply can feed through to raw-material prices with a delay, and the IEA's view that petrochemical feedstocks drive most 2027 demand growth links the oil balance directly to the chemical value chain. Points that may be worth considering include the IEA's next report, naphtha and other feedstock prices and Gulf export volumes.

The Guardian | Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Anadolu Agency | Lianhe Zaobao | Cinco Días | Dawn

item.title: The Spanish chemical industry federation Feique expects 2026 production to grow 1.5% and turnover 3.8% to EUR 88.633 billion, mainly on higher prices, while exports are expected to fall 6% in value.
item.description:
The Spanish Chemical Industry Business Federation (Feique) expects the chemical industry, defined as statistical classes CNAE 20 and 21, to close 2026 with production growth of 1.5% and turnover up 3.8% to EUR 88.633 billion, mainly because of higher prices. Exports are expected to fall 6% in value despite a slight increase in exported volumes, which Feique attributes to rising international competitive pressure, production overcapacity and the tariff policies of third countries. Basic chemistry has accumulated a 20% drop in production since 2021, against growth of 30% in pharmaceutical chemistry and 20% in consumer and specialty chemistry, Feique says; the row does not state the period for these growth figures. The row does not give the 2025 base figures, the size of the price effect, 2026 production by sub-sector, which countries' tariffs are meant, or the export volume change in numbers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives an industry federation's estimate for the full year, not final data, and turnover that rises mainly on prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a gap between price-led turnover growth and modest production growth points to cost pass-through rather than stronger demand, and a long decline in basic chemistry can mean less local supply of intermediates. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Spanish and other European producers supply raw materials and additives to formulators, so a shrinking basic chemistry base and price-led selling can affect raw-material availability and prices; the row gives no product-level figures. Points that may be worth considering include Feique's final 2026 data, basic chemistry output and European export prices.

Feique
